options: It reliably prints "5 7" with -O0 and "5 8" with -O2.
The behavior is undefined; different builds may print different results or anything at all.
It reliably prints "5 8" on all optimizing compilers.
It fails to compile because modifying a variable twice on one line is a syntax error.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The expression i++ + ++i modifies i more than once between sequence points, which is undefined behavior in C. A conforming implementation may produce any output, or even optimize in surprising ways, and still be correct by the standard.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Many learners memorize a particular compiler's output, but UB has no guaranteed result. B: Optimizations can change outcomes for UB, but there is no rule that ties results to -O levels. D: It's legal syntax; the issue is semantic undefined behavior, not a parse error.

options: The behavior is undefined due to fallthrough.
concept_mcqs.explanation: n == 2 selects case 2; there is no break, so execution continues into default. Starting from x=1: x*=3 gives 3, then default subtracts 1 to give 2.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Assumes case 1 runs (adding 10) before case 2, but control starts at the matching label, not from the top. C: Assumes all cases run including case 1, 2, and default applied to the original x; but case 1 is skipped because n != 1. D: Fallthrough is defined in C; it's not UB. It only surprises if you expect implicit breaks.

options: It prints 3 2 1 0 and terminates normally.
It fails to compile because comparing an unsigned to 0 is illegal.
It prints 3 2 1 0, then underflows to a large value and continues forever.
It prints 3 2 1 and skips 0 because the condition is evaluated before the body.
concept_mcqs.explanation: For unsigned types, i >= 0 is always true. After printing 0, --i wraps to UINT_MAX, and the loop continues indefinitely, printing many values.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: True for signed counters, but unsigned comparison with 0 never becomes false. C: Legal in C; unsigned comparisons are well-defined. D: The body executes before the condition check only in do-while; here it's a for-loop with a standard condition.

options: 0, because (b == 0) is evaluated first, then a & 0 is 0.
1, because a & b is 1 which is logically true.
It is implementation-defined; precedence between & and == varies by compiler.
1, because & has higher precedence than == so (a & b) == 0 is true.
concept_mcqs.explanation: Equality (==) binds tighter than bitwise AND (&), so the expression is parsed as a & (b == 0). Since b == 0 is false (0), the result is a & 0, which is 0, and printing with %d yields 0.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Assumes (a & b) is used as a logical condition, but the precedence causes a different grouping. C: The precedence claim is backward; == binds tighter than & in C. D: Operator precedence is fixed by the C standard; it's not implementation-defined.

concept_mcqs.explanation: x++ yields 1 (true) then increments x to 2. The true branch y++ yields 2 then increments y to 3. So x=2, y=3, z=2.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Treats z as the incremented y and leaves x unincremented. C: Confuses pre/post increment timing. D: Adds an extra increment to z or mis-evaluates the branch result.

options: It blocks waiting for input because %c skips whitespace.
concept_mcqs.explanation: %d consumes the 5, leaving the space in the stream. %c does not skip whitespace, so it reads that space, whose code is 32 on POSIX. Thus it prints 5-32.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Assumes %c will read 'x', but it takes the next byte, which is the space. C: Assumes the next byte is a newline code, but the provided bytes are space then 'x'. D: %c never skips whitespace; only formats with a leading space or %d/%s do.

concept_mcqs.explanation: a/b is integer division (2), which is then cast to double, yielding 2.0 for d1. Casting a to double before division yields floating division 5.0/2 = 2.5 for d2.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A and C: Mix up where the cast occurs. D: Assumes both divisions are integer before any cast, which is only true for d1.

options: Undefined behavior because assignment in conditions is illegal.
concept_mcqs.explanation: On each iteration, count is assigned i % 2, then used as the condition. i=0 sets count=0 (false). i=1 sets count=1 (true) then ++count makes it 2. i=2 sets count=0 again (false). Final count is 0.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B or C: Both ignore the final assignment on i=2 that resets count to 0. D: Assignment in conditions is legal in C; it's a common source of logic bugs, not UB.

scenario_questions.task: Explain precisely why this control flow is broken for unsigned types, what happens at n = 0 and in general at i == 0, and propose two safe iteration patterns that cover the same intent without undefined or unintended behavior. Justify when each is preferable.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
Problem: size_t is unsigned. If n == 0, computing n - 1 underflows before the loop even begins, yielding a very large value; the loop then likely runs "forever". Even for n > 0, i >= 0 is always true for unsigned, so after i reaches 0 and is decremented, it wraps to SIZE_MAX and the loop continues.
Two safe patterns:
1) Use the well-known i-- > 0 test that avoids comparing to 0 directly:

```c
for (size_t i = n; i-- > 0; ) {
    /* i goes from n-1 down to 0 exactly once */
}
```
This never evaluates i >= 0; the post-decrement compares the prior value to 0.
2) If negative indices are valid logic, use a signed type sized appropriately:

```c
for (long long i = (long long)n - 1; i >= 0; --i) { /* ... */ }
```
This uses a signed comparison that can become false. Choose a signed type wide enough for n.
Alternatively, an ascending loop is simplest and avoids pitfalls:

```c
for (size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) { /* ... */ }
```
Prefer ascending when order doesn’t matter; prefer the i-- > 0 idiom when descending order is required over an unsigned domain.

rubric.criterion: Explains unsigned wraparound and why i>=0 is always true for unsigned
Analyzes the n==0 case and initialization underflow clearly
Provides two correct, idiomatic alternatives (e.g., i-- > 0 and/or ascending loop or signed index)
Justifies when to choose each alternative

scenario_questions.task: Identify the cause and propose at least two minimal, correct fixes. For each, explain why it works and any trade-offs. Do not change to file I/O or add libraries.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
Cause: After reading the integer, the newline from pressing Enter remains in stdin. %c does not skip whitespace, so it reads that '\n', which is not 'y'.
Fixes:
- Whitespace in the format string to skip leading whitespace:

```c
scanf(" %c", &ans);  // leading space tells scanf to skip any whitespace
```
Trade-off: still uses scanf; be mindful of unchecked return values.
- Consume the rest of the line explicitly, then read the answer:

```c
int ch;
while ((ch = getchar()) != '\n' && ch != EOF) { }
ans = getchar();
```
Trade-off: Two reads; you must handle EOF carefully. Use int for getchar.
- Or prompt for the answer with a conversion that skips whitespace inherently, e.g., using %1s into a char buffer and taking the first char; but the simplest in this context is the leading space in "%c".
All fixes rely on understanding that whitespace handling differs between %c and numeric formats and that getchar returns int for EOF.

rubric.criterion: Correctly identifies the leftover newline as the cause and explains %c whitespace behavior
Proposes a correct scanf-based fix using a leading space and explains why it works
Proposes a second correct fix using getchar (with int) and explains EOF/ordering concerns

concept_mcqs.explanation: In main, a is an array of 10 ints: sizeof(a) = 10 * 4 = 40. In f, the parameter a is adjusted to int*, so sizeof(a) is the size of a pointer (8 on LP64).
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Confuses element count (10) with bytes and still recognizes pointer decay. C: Assumes arrays don't decay in parameters. D: Doubly confuses bytes with element count and misses decay.

options: It reliably prints an empty string
Undefined behavior
It reliably prints "OK"

concept_mcqs.explanation: The function returns a pointer to a dead stack object; any use is undefined behavior. A print might appear to work or crash; neither is guaranteed.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Observed on some runs but not guaranteed. C: A specific outcome with no basis. D: Many compilers accept this; the error is semantic, not a required compile-time diagnostic.

concept_mcqs.stem:
You have this project:

```text
util.h
util.c
main.c
```

util.h contains a full function definition:

```c
// util.h
#include <stddef.h>
int sum(const int *a, size_t n) { int s = 0; for (size_t i=0;i<n;i++) s+=a[i]; return s; }
```

Both util.c and main.c include util.h. Linking fails with multiple definitions of sum. Which change fixes the link error while keeping exactly one externally visible definition?
options: Make the function static in util.h
Move the function body into util.c and leave only a prototype in util.h
Put extern before the definition in util.h and keep the body there
Add include guards to util.h
concept_mcqs.explanation: A single external definition should live in one .c; the header should only declare it. Include guards only prevent duplicate inclusion within one translation unit, not across different TUs. static changes linkage (not one shared definition). extern with a body is still a definition.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Guards don't stop two separate TUs each defining the function. C: Would link, but changes API to internal linkage and creates per-TU copies. D: extern does not negate that a definition is emitted in each TU.

options: Undefined behavior; often a crash due to read-only storage
It compiles and runs but silently ignores the write
It always causes a compile-time error in standard C
It works and the literal becomes "Hi"
concept_mcqs.explanation: String literals have static storage duration and attempting to modify them is undefined behavior. Commonly they reside in read-only memory and the program faults when writing.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Modifying string literals is not allowed. C: There's no defined silent ignore. D: Many compilers accept it; the failure is not mandated at compile time.

concept_mcqs.explanation: A static local retains its value between calls. c starts at 0 once, then pre-increment prints 1 then 2.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Thinks initialization occurs on each call before increment. C: Forgets the increment. D: Misunderstands both static lifetime and increment.

concept_mcqs.explanation: In main, sizeof(x)=5 bytes. In len, parameter s is a pointer, sizeof(s)=8 on LP64, so 8-1=7. This illustrates array-to-pointer decay and why sizeof can't measure string length in a function parameter.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Assumes sizeof(s) equals array size from caller. C/D: Mix up character count with bytes, and ignore pointer decay.

concept_mcqs.explanation: For a true 2D array, the compiler must know the second dimension to compute element addresses. Using a fixed column size in the parameter matches the declaration. B is wrong because int** is not compatible with int (*)[4]. C loses 2D shape and requires manual indexing with rows*cols. D would need VLA parameters with rows/cols earlier in the parameter list and is not written correctly here.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: A common but incorrect assumption that a 2D array is an int**. C: Tempting if you think decay erases all dimensions for free indexing. D: Looks modern but is syntactically and semantically wrong as written.

concept_mcqs.explanation: You can store at most n-1 characters and then write the terminator at index n-1. The loop condition ensures the last write is within bounds.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Omits the terminator, risking consumers reading past the buffer. C: Casts away const and still writes out of bounds at s[n]. D: Still writes s[n] inside the loop and again after, overflowing.

options: Compile silently; behavior is only undefined at runtime
Compile both and defer the problem to the linker
Succeed only on LP64 but fail on ILP32
Emit a compile-time diagnostic about conflicting types for idx_of
concept_mcqs.explanation: Including the header exposes a conflicting declaration versus the definition; the compiler must diagnose the mismatch.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Linkers see only symbol names, but the compiler must reject conflicting types. C: UB arises when calls don't match prototypes, but here the conflict is in one TU. D: ABI width doesn't rescue a type mismatch.

options: It is undefined behavior
It is well-defined: yields the element distance across arrays
It always prints 4 on flat address spaces
It is implementation-defined but safe to rely on
concept_mcqs.explanation: Pointer subtraction is defined only for pointers into the same array (or one past). Across different arrays it is undefined behavior.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: A common but incorrect intuition based on addresses. C: Not merely implementation-defined; it's UB. D: Coincidental on some platforms, not guaranteed.

scenario_questions.task: Identify precisely why this is undefined behavior and specify two concrete changes that eliminate the risk across platforms and compilers. Explain how headers, prototypes, and array-to-pointer decay inform your fixes. Mention any build settings that would have caught this earlier.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
The call site compiled with a mismatched prototype (src not const; parameter types and promotions may differ). Because main.c didn't include the authoritative header, the compiler assumed a different signature. The call is undefined behavior when the actual definition's calling convention and argument types don't match what the caller generated.

Two changes:
1) Include the real header in main.c and delete the local prototype:

```c
#include "strutil.h"
```

2) Enforce warnings-as-errors for mismatched or missing prototypes (e.g., compile with -Wall -Wextra -Werror and possibly -Wmissing-prototypes) so such issues are caught.

Optionally, make the API const-correct and keep size parameters explicit:

```c
size_t safe_copy(char *dst, size_t dstsz, const char *src);
```

Rationale: Function parameters that are arrays decay to pointers at the call site; only the prototype in the header defines the true types. Including the header ensures both caller and callee agree on the signature, preventing UB from ABI mismatches.

rubric.criterion: Accurate identification of the root cause: mismatched prototype due to not including the header
Two concrete and correct fixes (include header/remove local prototype; stricter compiler flags)
Sound reasoning tying in prototypes, const-correctness, and array-to-pointer decay

options: It will always print "Bob" and exit normally because `b` holds its own copy of the string.
It only leaks memory (no crash) because the second `free` is ignored by the allocator.

Undefined behavior: `b.name` becomes a dangling pointer after `free(a.name)`, so the `printf` is a use-after-free and the later `free(b.name)` is a double free. It might print "Bob", crash, or do anything.
It will always crash on the `printf` because reading freed memory is immediately trapped by the OS.
concept_mcqs.explanation: `Person b = a;` copies the pointer value, not the allocation it points to. After `free(a.name)`, both `a.name` and `b.name` point to freed storage. The `printf` reads freed memory (use-after-free), and `free(b.name)` attempts to free the same block again (double free). Both are undefined behavior; you might see a print then abort, or an immediate crash, or seemingly normal behavior depending on allocator/ASan/UB luck.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: A shallow copy does not create a second allocation; believing it does is a common error. C: Some sanitizers abort here, but the OS does not universally trap reads of freed heap memory; UB is not guaranteed immediate crash. D: Many allocators detect double frees and abort; ignoring a double free is not the specified behavior and still UB.

options: Undefined behavior due to heap buffer overflow; the program may print an arbitrary value or crash.
Compile-time error because `sizeof` cannot be applied to pointers.
Works correctly but wastes memory because `sizeof arr` is larger than `sizeof(Node)`.
Works because `sizeof arr` equals `sizeof *arr` after decay in `sizeof` expressions.
concept_mcqs.explanation: `sizeof arr` is the size of the pointer (`Node*`), not the pointee. If `sizeof(Node)` (commonly 16) is larger than `sizeof(Node*)` (commonly 8), the allocation is too small (80 bytes for 10 elements instead of 160). The writes overflow the heap buffer; result is UB.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: The claim is inverted; it under-allocates, not over-allocates. C: `sizeof` does not cause decay; `sizeof *arr` is correct, `sizeof arr` is not. D: `sizeof` applies to any type or expression, including pointers.

options: Safe sentinel write because flexible arrays reserve an extra byte automatically.
Safe as long as `n` is even, due to alignment padding at the end of the allocation.
Out-of-bounds write (one past the allocated space), invoking undefined behavior.
Defined but implementation-defined; the C standard guarantees space for one extra element.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The allocation is exactly `sizeof(Packet) + n` bytes beyond the header, so valid indices are `0..n-1`. Writing at index `n` is one past the end and UB. Flexible array members do not automatically add a sentinel slot.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B/D: Common misconceptions. The standard requires you to allocate exactly as much as you will use; it does not add an extra element. C: Alignment/padding at the struct level does not create guaranteed writable space after the flexible array payload.

options: Well-defined if compiled with optimizations; otherwise undefined.
Undefined behavior: `p` points to a dead stack frame; access may appear to work but is invalid.
Well-defined: the compiler performs copy elision of the local and extends its lifetime.
Defined as long as `Item` contains only POD (plain old data).
concept_mcqs.explanation: The function returns the address of a block-scope object whose lifetime ends at function return. The pointer becomes indeterminate, and dereferencing is UB. C does not extend the lifetime of locals or apply copy elision here.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: C does not do copy elision across function boundaries for locals like this. C: Optimizations do not legitimize UB. D: POD-ness is irrelevant in C; lifetime rules still apply.

concept_mcqs.explanation: `c` occupies 1 byte; then 3 bytes of padding are inserted to align `x` at offset 4. The structure ends after `x` at total size 8, which is already a multiple of 4. Thus `offsetof(S,x)=4` and `sizeof(S)=8`.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B/D: Ignore required padding before `x`. C: Suggests extra tail padding to 12; not needed because 8 is already a multiple of `int`'s alignment on LP64 in this layout.

options: Undefined behavior: `p` may be invalid after `realloc`; writing through it can corrupt memory.
Safe: `realloc` never moves the block when growing, it only extends in place.
Safe as long as we read, but not if we write, through `p`. Reads do not invalidate caches.
Safe in this case because we grew by a multiple of the old size, preserving addresses.
concept_mcqs.explanation: `realloc` may move the allocation to a new address. Any pointer into the old block (like `p`) becomes invalid if the block moves. Using it is UB regardless of read or write.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B/C: `realloc` is allowed to move; multiples and sizes do not guarantee in-place growth. D: Reads through an invalid pointer are also UB; caching is irrelevant.

options: No leak: on failure `realloc` leaves `b->buf` unchanged by specification.
UB only if `b->cap` is not a power of two; otherwise safe.
Double free risk, but only if `free` is called immediately after `grow`.
Leak and loss of the original buffer: `realloc` returns NULL and overwrites `b->buf`, losing the only pointer.
concept_mcqs.explanation: On failure, `realloc` returns NULL and leaves the original block allocated and untouched. Overwriting `b->buf` with NULL loses the only reference to that allocation, causing a leak and data loss. The correct pattern is to assign to a temporary and check for NULL before updating `b->buf`.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: It's true that the original pointer is unchanged internally, but this code overwrites the only variable holding it, causing the leak. C: Power-of-two capacity is irrelevant. D: The immediate problem is the lost pointer; double free is not implied here.

options: `dup_shallow` yields double-free/UB on names; `dup_deep` is correct if all `strdup` calls succeed.
`dup_deep` still risks double-free because `strdup` shares the same underlying bytes when the strings are equal.
Both are safe as long as you free the arrays themselves with a single `free` each afterwards.
`dup_shallow` is safe if the strings are short (fit in the small-string optimization).
concept_mcqs.explanation: `dup_shallow` copies the pointers, so original and duplicate reference the same allocations; freeing both causes double frees. `dup_deep` allocates new copies so freeing each element in each array is correct, assuming all `strdup` succeed (check for NULL in production).
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Frees of the arrays do not fix the duplicated inner pointers. C: `strdup` always allocates new storage; there is no SSO in C strings. D: There is no small-string optimization in C's `malloc`/`strdup` behavior.

options: It prints garbage because structs cannot be passed by value when they have pointers.
It prints "Eli" because `set_name` updates the caller's struct field.
It always crashes because `free(p.name)` frees `a.name` in the caller and then `a.name` is used.
Undefined behavior if `strdup` fails; otherwise it prints "Ana" and leaks or double-frees depend on later code.
concept_mcqs.explanation: The parameter `p` is a copy. `free(p.name)` frees the same allocation as `a.name`, but the caller's `a.name` still holds the dangling pointer. The assignment to `p.name` does not update `a.name`. The `printf` prints the old value "Ana" (UB was invoked earlier by freeing and then later using `a.name`), and freeing `a.name` again can double-free. If `strdup` fails, there's UB from freeing then leaking. The key point: pass-by-value does not update the caller's field.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: Would require passing `Person*` or returning the updated struct. C: A crash is not guaranteed; UB may or may not manifest immediately. D: Structs can be passed by value; pointer members do not forbid it.

options: No risk: `memmove` fully solves overlapping copies of structs with pointers.
Logical aliasing of internal pointers causes multiple elements to point to the same `name`, leading to double frees.
`memmove` corrupts the integer `id` fields only when the shift distance is 1.
Only a memory leak is possible; double free cannot occur because addresses are unique.
concept_mcqs.explanation: `memmove` is correct for overlapping copies at the byte level, but it does not deep-copy. After shifting, multiple elements can end up holding identical `name` pointers. Freeing each element's `name` exactly once then double-frees the same allocations. A content-aware deep shift is required if ownership must be preserved per element.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: `memmove` preserves bytes; integer corruption is not specific to distance. C: It solves overlap at the outer struct level, not ownership semantics of inner pointers. D: The aliasing precisely enables double frees when freeing each element's `name`.

scenario_questions.task: Identify all allocation/size-of errors in the snippet that can cause out-of-bounds access during `qsort`, explain why they manifest in sorting, and provide the precise one-line fixes. Also mention any secondary risks you see with the current code.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
Two `sizeof` errors:

1) `Person *p = malloc(n * sizeof p);` allocates `n * sizeof(Person*)`, not `n * sizeof(Person)`. On 64-bit, this under-allocates, and subsequent writes to `p[i]` overflow.
2) `qsort(p, n, sizeof p, cmp_person);` passes the size of a pointer, not `sizeof(Person)`, causing the sorter to treat elements as smaller than they are and step through memory with the wrong stride, reading/writing out of bounds.

Fixes (two lines):

```c
Person *p = malloc(n * sizeof *p);
qsort(p, n, sizeof *p, cmp_person);
```

Why it shows in sorting: `qsort` moves elements assuming the provided element size; a wrong, smaller size causes overlapping moves and out-of-bounds reads/writes, quickly detected by ASan. The under-sized allocation magnifies the issue because even correct element sizes would still overflow the buffer when filling or moving.

Secondary risks: missing NULL checks on allocations; repeated identical `name` strings do not cause correctness issues but may stress comparisons; potential leak if `load_people` fails partway through without cleanup.

rubric.criterion: Correctly identifies both `sizeof` mistakes (in `malloc` and in `qsort`)
Explains clearly how each mistake leads to out-of-bounds behavior during sorting
Provides exact corrected code for both lines (`sizeof *p`)
Notes at least one secondary robustness issue (e.g., NULL checks, partial allocation rollback)

scenario_questions.task: Evaluate the safety of allowing clients to cache raw `Record*` pointers as stable identifiers. If unsafe, propose a design that preserves stability while still using a contiguous dynamic array internally. Justify with precise failure modes and concrete changes to the API and data structures.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
Caching raw `Record*` is unsafe because `realloc` may move the array, invalidating all cached pointers (dangling). Additionally, removals that compact by `memmove` change element addresses, invalidating pointers to subsequent elements. Failure modes: use-after-free, writing through dangling pointers corrupting memory.

Safer designs:

- Indirect via indices plus generation counters: expose a lightweight handle `{size_t index; uint32_t gen;}`. Store a `gen` per slot in the array. On removal, increment `gen`. Clients validate that `handle.gen == recs[index].gen` before use. Moving elements updates their `gen` or invalidates stale handles. No raw pointer exposure.

- Or use a stable indirection table: keep `Record **slots` (vector of pointers to heap-allocated `Record`s). Expose `RecordID` as an index into `slots`. Growing `slots` via `realloc` does not move the `Record` allocations themselves; compaction swaps `slots[i]` values without changing underlying `Record*`. Destruction frees the pointed `Record` and sets `slots[i]=NULL`.

With a contiguous `Record recs[]` requirement, prefer the index+generation handle: keep `recs` as a normal dynamic array; on remove, swap-with-last and decrement `len` to minimize memmoves, update a side-car `gen[]`, and return updated indices to clients as needed. API change: functions accept/return `RecordHandle` instead of `Record*`; lookup validates the handle, returning `Record*` transiently for immediate use, not for caching.

These preserve stability at the handle level and prevent dangling raw pointers across `realloc` and compaction.

rubric.criterion: Identifies why caching raw `Record*` is unsafe under `realloc` and compaction (dangling/use-after-free)
Proposes a specific stable indirection (index+generation or pointer table) and explains how it prevents invalidation
Explains required API/data-structure changes concretely (handle type, validation, side-car arrays or slots)
Discusses element removal/growth implications and how the proposal handles them (swap-with-last, gen bump, or slots updates)

options: It loops forever
Undefined behavior due to fscanf
concept_mcqs.explanation: feof(fp) is only set after a read attempt hits EOF. The last fscanf fails to convert and sets the EOF indicator. ferror(fp) is still 0, so count++ executes one extra time before the loop exits. With three integers, it prints 4.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Many assume !feof is a correct read loop and forget the extra iteration on the EOF-triggering read. C: fscanf failing to match is not undefined behavior; it returns EOF without setting ferror. D: The feof condition will eventually become true after the failed read, so it won’t loop forever.

options: Behavior is undefined; an intervening fflush/seek is required before the read
It blocks waiting for a newline because of line buffering
[abc]
concept_mcqs.explanation: After writing, the C standard requires an intervening fflush or a file-positioning call (fseek/rewind/fsetpos) before doing a read on the same stream. Without it, behavior is undefined.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: It looks plausible if you think the file position advanced as expected. B: An empty read is a common observed outcome but it’s not guaranteed. D: Line buffering affects terminal streams; here the stream is a file and the issue is mixing I/O without a flush/seek.

options: process receives uninitialized data for the first record
It skips the last record due to buffer reuse
Nothing; this is the correct EOF check for fread
It loops forever at EOF because fread returns 0, not EOF
concept_mcqs.explanation: fread returns a count (0 or 1 here). At EOF/short read it returns 0. Comparing that to EOF (-1) yields true, so the loop never terminates. The correct condition is while (fread(...) == 1).
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: A reused buffer can be a problem elsewhere but here the logic error is the termination check. C: This is a common confusion with getc-style APIs that return EOF. D: The first record is read before the check; uninitialized data is not the primary fault.

options: Prints 12 and exits successfully
errno becomes EINVAL and it prints "invalid"
Undefined behavior due to NULL endptr
Prints "invalid" because of the trailing 'x'
concept_mcqs.explanation: strtol stops at the first non-digit and returns the parsed prefix (12). errno remains 0 unless overflow/underflow occurs. Detecting non-numeric suffix requires inspecting the endptr.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A/D: Both assume strtol sets errno on non-numeric suffix; it does not. C: Passing NULL for endptr is defined if you don’t need to know where parsing stopped.

options: It prints "opened: Success" because successful fopen resets errno to 0
strerror may return NULL, so output is implementation-defined
It prints "opened: Permission denied" because errno is unchanged on success
Undefined behavior: reading errno after success is UB
concept_mcqs.explanation: Library functions are not required to modify errno on success. Using errno without an error return reads a stale value. The program will likely print the old message.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Common misconception; many APIs leave errno untouched on success. C: strerror returns a pointer to a string; NULL is not a standard outcome here. D: It’s not UB to read errno; it’s just meaningless unless a function signals an error.

options: Move the second fputs before fclose or reopen the file before writing again
Set fp = NULL after fclose and keep using it
Insert fflush(fp) before the second fputs
Do not call fclose; rely on program exit to flush
concept_mcqs.explanation: After fclose, fp is invalid. The correct fix is to avoid using a closed stream: either write before closing or reopen a new stream for the subsequent write.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: fflush doesn’t resurrect a closed stream. B: Avoiding fclose hides the bug and can leak resources; it’s not a correct fix pattern. C: Writing to NULL just crashes differently; it does not fix the misuse.

options: Call fflush(fp) before fseek
Open with mode "rb" instead of "r"
Subtract the number of '\n' characters from sz
Use SEEK_CUR instead of SEEK_END
concept_mcqs.explanation: In text mode, the runtime may translate CRLF to LF, so the logical position does not equal byte count. Opening in binary mode ("rb") disables translation and makes ftell reflect bytes on disk.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: B: fflush is about output buffers, not input translation. C: Counting newlines is neither reliable nor portable. D: The origin constant does not address text translation issues.

options: It reliably discards any pending input so scanf reads a fresh number
It’s a defined no-op on input streams
scanf will fail with EINVAL after fflush(stdin)
Undefined behavior; fflush is only defined on output/update streams
concept_mcqs.explanation: The C standard defines fflush only for output or update streams. Calling it on an input-only stream like stdin is undefined behavior.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A/C/D: All are common beliefs or platform-specific behaviors, but none are guaranteed by the C standard.

options: Use fmemopen to create a failing stream for fputs
Refactor to inject a write operation (function pointer) so the test can force a failure
Use tmpfile, then close its underlying descriptor before fputs to force EOF
Mount a read-only directory and write there during the test
concept_mcqs.explanation: Standard C does not provide a way to force fputs to fail on a real FILE reliably. Introducing a seam (e.g., a function pointer or wrapper around fputs) lets a test double simulate failure deterministically.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: Standard C doesn’t expose a safe way to invalidate the FILE’s descriptor. B: Environment-dependent and brittle. D: fmemopen is not standard C (it’s POSIX/GNU), and it doesn’t inherently fail writes.

options: Call setvbuf(stdout, NULL, _IONBF, 0) before fopen
Assign stdout = f; then printf goes to the file
Use freopen("out.txt", "w", stdout);
Call dup2 on fileno(stdout) to fileno(f) in portable C
concept_mcqs.explanation: freopen with stdout is the standard, portable way to re-associate stdout with a file stream in C. After that, printf writes to the file.
concept_mcqs.distractor_rationale: A: stdout is not meant to be reassigned; doing so is undefined. C: Buffering mode doesn’t redirect the stream. D: dup2 is POSIX, not portable standard C.

scenario_questions.task: Propose a design and justify it. Specify the correct file-opening modes and the exact I/O sequence to avoid data loss, including how you will handle validation failures. Describe how you would unit test both the success path and the first-failure path without touching production data. State the return codes you will use and what each means.
scenario_questions.expected_answer:
Open the source for reading only and write to a separate temporary output file in the same directory. Example: src = fopen(path, "r"); tmp = fopen("<path>.tmp", "w"). Read each line from src with fgets, validate using a parser that returns a status; if invalid, abort the import: close tmp, remove the temp file, leave the original file untouched, and return a specific error code (e.g., 2). If valid, write the normalized line to tmp using fputs/fwrite and check return values and ferror. After a successful pass with no invalid lines and no write errors, fclose both streams, then atomically replace the original via rename("<path>.tmp", path). On platforms with non-atomic rename-overwrite semantics, handle EEXIST by removing the target or ensure the destination doesn’t exist beforehand.
To avoid mixing I/O on a single stream, never read from the file opened in write mode; use distinct FILE*s and do not read-after-write without fflush/seek. Ensure errors are surfaced: return 1 when the input cannot be opened, 2 for validation failure (and clean up the temp file), 3 for write error (detect via ferror or fputs == EOF), 4 for rename failure, 0 on success.
For testing, separate parsing/normalization into pure functions that take a string and return a normalized string plus a status, so they can be unit tested without files. For the import integration, run tests against copies of fixtures in a temp directory; verify that on invalid input the original file is unchanged and the temp file is removed; on success, verify output matches golden data. To simulate write failures deterministically, wrap fputs/fwrite behind an injectable function pointer or interface so a test double can force a failure to hit the write-error path.

rubric.criterion: Explains why opening with "w+" corrupts the input and identifies the need for separate input and output streams
Specifies safe I/O sequence with correct modes ("r" for input, "w" for temp output), checks for errors, and avoids mixing IO without flush/seek
Describes failure handling that preserves the original file (cleanup temp on failure, atomic rename on success) and maps clear return codes
Outlines a test strategy separating parsing from I/O and explains how to test success and failure (including a deterministic write-failure seam)

scenario_questions.task: Identify the root cause and provide the corrected sequence of I/O operations, including any necessary flushing, repositioning, truncation, or validation. Justify each step and discuss how you would make this testable.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Root cause: After reading the number, the file position is at the end of the parsed token, not necessarily at the start. Writing without repositioning overwrites from the current position, leaving the old digits in place if the new representation is shorter/longer, and may append after the original if there is leftover content. Mixing input and output on an update stream also requires an intervening fflush or reposition call per C. Correct sequence: open with "r+" (or create with "w+" if missing, handled separately), read the number using fgets + strtol with endptr validation to ensure only digits and optional newline exist; then call fseek(f, 0, SEEK_SET) to reposition; optionally call fflush(f) after the read (strict conformance) or rely on the fseek as the required positioning call; write the new number with fprintf; then call fflush(f) and, if the new text can be shorter than the old, call ftruncate via platform API or rewrite to a fresh temp file scheme (portable approach: write to a temp file and rename). For strict portability, prefer the temp file approach over truncation. For testing, extract parse_number(const char*) and format_number(long, char*, size_t) as pure functions and test them with unit tests; for integration, test with a temp directory and verify exact file contents before/after, including edge cases where digit count changes.

rubric.criterion: Correctly identifies mixing I/O without reposition and the need to seek before writing
Proposes a valid, standard-conforming sequence (read with validation; fseek/rewind; write; flush) and explains why each step is necessary
Addresses variable-length write issue (truncate or temp-file+rename) with a justified, portable solution
Proposes a test plan separating parsing/formatting and exercising integration with temp files

scenario_questions.task: Explain precisely why the last line is lost and propose a corrected loop that is robust to missing trailing newlines and avoids feof misuse. Include any extra validation needed and how you would test this fix.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: Problem: Using while (!feof(fi)) with fgets is a classic anti-pattern. feof only becomes true after a read attempt hits EOF. In a one-line, no-newline file, the first fgets succeeds, but the logic places the fgets inside the loop controlled by feof, which initially is false; if the code hits a corner where the conditional flow breaks early, you can easily miss the line. The robust idiom is to use fgets as the loop condition: while (fgets(buf, sizeof buf, fi)) { ... }. With this change, the single line is processed regardless of a trailing newline. Also, the filter condition should not assume a newline terminator; check for non-empty content via buf[0] != '\0' and optionally strip the trailing newline if present. Tests: add cases for empty file, single line without newline, lines with only "\n", and a long line exceeding the buffer to ensure partial reads are handled per requirements (e.g., skip or handle continuation).

rubric.criterion: Correctly identifies feof misuse and explains the EOF indicator timing
Provides a correct fgets-controlled loop and explains why it fixes the missing-line case
Addresses newline/no-newline handling and content validation clearly
Proposes test cases covering no-newline, empty, and long-line scenarios

scenario_questions.task: Diagnose the fault and propose a robust fix that preserves performance. Explain how you would validate the fix with unit tests and what invariants those tests assert.
scenario_questions.expected_answer: The buffer from fread is not null-terminated; passing it to strcmp/strncmp-based logic assumes a C string. strcmp reads until a '\0', which may read past the buffer end when n == 64 or when the data lacks a terminator within bounds, causing UB and crashes. Fixes: either ensure null termination (e.g., read at most sizeof(buf) - 1 bytes and write buf[n] = '\0' after fread) or refactor classify_line to accept a (ptr,len) pair and never call strcmp—use memcmp against fixed prefixes and length checks (e.g., n >= 4 && memcmp(s, "INFO", 4) == 0). Prefer the latter for robustness and performance, avoiding repeated scans for '\0'. Unit tests: provide inputs with and without embedded NULs, exactly full buffers (n == sizeof(buf) - 1 and == sizeof(buf)), and varying prefixes; assert no out-of-bounds reads (can be checked with sanitizers) and correct classification. Invariants: functions that take (ptr,len) never read past ptr+len; string-based versions always enforce an explicit terminator before calling strcmp.

rubric.criterion: Accurately identifies the missing NUL terminator and why strcmp/strncmp cause UB
Proposes a robust, performant fix (either enforce termination or use length-based comparisons) with concrete details
Describes unit tests that cover boundary conditions (exactly full reads, embedded NULs, prefixes)

I/O code uses safe patterns: fgets as loop condition or fread with explicit length checks; no fflush on input; no mixing read/write on one stream without reposition.
README includes: build commands, how to run tests, sample input and exact expected output, and a short note describing a debugging session (the bug, the symptom, the fix).

rubric.criterion: Modular design with clear interfaces (parser, aggregator, CLI) and no global mutable state leaks
Correct, robust parsing using (ptr,len) or explicit NUL-termination; proper status codes for invalid data
Accurate aggregation and CLI behavior, including documented exit codes and correct formatting of output
Comprehensive tests that run non-interactively and catch edge cases; failing tests cause non-zero exit
Demonstrated debugging: a described failure reproduced and fixed, with the fix reflected in code/tests/README
